questions.q: In SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS, what does the CI flag mean?
options: Case-insensitive — 'Smith' and 'smith' compare as equal
Case-intensive — case differences are amplified
Code-independent — the collation ignores character encoding
Column-indexed — the collation only applies to indexed columns
questions.explain: CI means case-insensitive comparison; CS would mean case-sensitive.

questions.q: In the same collation name, what does the AS flag mean?
options: Accent-sensitive — 'café' and 'cafe' compare as different
Auto-sort — the collation determines default ORDER BY behavior only
ASCII-only — the collation rejects non-ASCII characters
Alphabet-strict — only Latin letters are permitted
questions.explain: AS means accent-sensitive; AI (accent-insensitive) would treat accented and unaccented characters as equal.

questions.q: Why can comparing character columns from two different collations cause a runtime error rather than just sorting differently?
options: SQL Server needs a single, unambiguous collation to compare two character values, and a mismatch is genuinely ambiguous
SQL Server always converts silently to the server default with no error
Collation only affects ORDER BY, never WHERE or JOIN comparisons
This only happens with numeric data types, never character types
questions.explain: SQL Server raises a 'Cannot resolve the collation conflict' error when it cannot determine which collation's rules should govern the comparison.

questions.q: Why do collation conflicts commonly show up with #temp tables specifically?
options: tempdb always uses the instance's default collation for object definitions, regardless of the user database's own collation
Temp tables cannot have any collation at all
Temp tables are stored in a different code page than permanent tables
Temp tables always use accent-insensitive collation by design
questions.explain: If a database's collation differs from the instance default, joining a #temp table (built in tempdb, using the instance default) back to that database's columns creates a mismatch.

questions.q: What is the standard fix for a collation conflict in a specific query?
options: Add an explicit COLLATE clause to force one side of the comparison to match the other
Restart the SQL Server instance
Drop and recreate tempdb
Change the query to use only numeric columns
questions.explain: COLLATE inline resolves the immediate ambiguity, though it's worth treating recurring COLLATE fixes as a sign something upstream should be revisited.
